samples.text:
Nowadays children see advertisements everywhere, on television, on the internet and even in their games. Some people think that all advertising for children who are under twelve should be banned. I completely agree with this idea.

The first reason is that young children cannot understand the purpose of advertising. They believe what they see on the screen and they don't know that the company only want to sell products. For example, if a child see an advert for a new toy with happy children playing, he thinks that he will be very happy if he gets it. Adults can think critically but children are not able to do this, so it is not fair to target them.

The second reason is that advertising can be bad for children's health. Many adverts for children are about sweets, fast food and sugary drinks. These products are very attractive with bright colours and cartoon characters, and children ask their parents to buy them. If they eat this kind of food too much, they can become overweight and have health problems in the future.

In addition, adverts create pressure on the parents. Children always want the newest toys and they cry or become angry if parents say no. Many families don't have enough money to buy everything, so this cause arguments at home. Also children can feel sad when their friends have things that they don't have.

Some people say that companies need to advertise to sell their products. However, they can still advertise to parents, because parents are the one who pay for the products.

In conclusion, I strongly believe that advertising aimed at children under twelve should be banned, because children cannot understand it and it can harm their health and their family life.

samples.text:
Children today are exposed to a constant stream of advertisements on television, websites and mobile games. As a result, there have been calls for a complete ban on advertising directed at children under twelve. I strongly agree with this proposal, since young children are especially vulnerable to persuasive marketing.

The main reason for my view is that young children lack the ability to recognise advertising for what it is. Before a certain age, many children cannot clearly distinguish between entertainment and a commercial message, and they tend to accept claims at face value. When a cartoon character they love tells them that a particular cereal will make them stronger, they are likely to believe it. Targeting an audience that cannot critically evaluate information is, in my opinion, fundamentally unfair.

Secondly, much of the advertising aimed at children promotes products that are harmful or unnecessary. Sugary snacks, fast food and expensive toys dominate children's channels and apps, and their marketing often relies on bright colours, free gifts and celebrity endorsements. This contributes to unhealthy eating habits and encourages a materialistic attitude from an early age. It also puts a considerable pressure on parents, who may face tantrums or feel guilty when they cannot afford the latest products.

Opponents argue that a ban would harm businesses and restrict freedom of expression. However, companies would still be able to market their products to parents, who are ultimately the ones making purchasing decisions. Moreover, several countries already restrict advertising to children, which suggests that such regulation is both practical and effective.

In conclusion, I firmly believe that all advertising aimed at children under twelve should be banned. Protecting young children from manipulation and unhealthy influences is more important than the commercial interests of advertisers.

samples.text:
Advertisers spend vast sums targeting children, whose influence over family spending is considerable. The suggestion that all advertising aimed at under-twelves should be prohibited is therefore a significant one, and I agree with it to a large extent, while recognising that a ban would need to be carefully defined to be workable.

The most compelling argument concerns children's cognitive development. Younger children often struggle to recognise the persuasive intent behind an advertisement and are inclined to accept its claims uncritically. Marketing techniques that would barely register with an adult, such as a favourite cartoon character endorsing a snack or a toy shown in an exaggeratedly exciting setting, can be highly effective on a seven-year-old. Directing such messages at an audience that cannot defend itself against them is difficult to justify ethically.

The consequences extend beyond the individual child. Advertising to children is dominated by foods high in sugar and fat, and repeated exposure shapes preferences that may persist into adulthood, with obvious implications for public health. It also fuels what is often called "pester power", placing parents under pressure to buy products they cannot afford or would not otherwise choose, and encouraging children to measure their worth by what they own.

Critics of a ban raise two points: that it would unfairly restrict legitimate businesses, and that parents, not governments, should protect their children. Yet firms would remain free to advertise to adults, who make the actual purchasing decisions, and the sheer volume of online marketing, much of it embedded in games and videos, makes parental supervision alone unrealistic.

The main practical challenge lies in enforcement, particularly on digital platforms where age and intent are harder to define. Clear rules on content designed to appeal to children would be essential.

In conclusion, I strongly support banning advertising aimed at children under twelve. Their vulnerability to persuasion outweighs the commercial arguments against such a restriction.
